content:
When formatting messages in the infoview which are not suggestions, we often do not want to format according to any specific width, as the infoview is responsible for wrapping content independently. However, MessageData is formatted according to the default width of 120, which results in the insertion of unexpected newlines in rich message data that occurs in sufficiently long messages.

The main proposal here is to make w := 0 in Std.Format.pretty correspond to infinite width, and never insert any extra newlines in that case. As far as I know we do not yet have a way to say "pretty print with infinite width", and this would fill that gap more generally.

The secondary proposal is to make infinite width the default when rendering MessageData.

Note: currently MessageData always uses the fixed default width. To actually have an effect on MessageData rendering, we'd need to either

  1. respect the option format.width during rendering
  2. use a fixed value of 0 when rendering message data
  3. make the default value of format.width 0
  4. some combination of "use 0 as the default" and "respect the given option" (e.g. respect the option and change the default value, or set the option to 0 in various settings, etc.)

Instances of this being asked about: #lean4 > pretty print format with no whitespace , #Editors & UIs > Width of MessageData in InfoView (VS Code) , this comment on #39296 (non-exhaustive)

Consider this example from #39296. The second logInfo truncates the message to show that this formatting is not inherent to pretty-printing, but depends on the length of the message.

import Lean

open Lean

/--
info: exact
  Nat.le_succ_of_le✝
    h✝ uses a rigid tactic. Previously, a flexible tactic, which potentially modified all hypotheses and the goal, was used.
---
info: exact Nat.le_succ_of_le✝ h✝ uses a rigid tactic.
-/
#guard_msgs in
run_cmd do
  let tacStx ← `(tactic| exact Nat.le_succ_of_le h)
  logInfo m!"{tacStx} uses a rigid tactic. Previously, a flexible tactic, which \
    potentially modified all hypotheses and the goal, was used."
  logInfo m!"{tacStx} uses a rigid tactic."

One thing I'd like to understand better before making this a real RFC is why we have format.width in the first place, and why it defaults to 120. For suggestions, after all, we refer to an entirely different option, format.inputWidth. (Note: I'd expect an autoformatter to use the same option as suggestions, whichever option that is.)

It seems to only affect the behavior of pretty' and pp.oneline (show only the first line of output). I can't find any uses of pretty' in core.

Thomas Murrills said:

For suggestions, after all, we refer to an entirely different option, format.inputWidth. (Note: I'd expect an autoformatter to use the same option as suggestions, whichever option that is.)

According to the docstring of format.inputWidth it "controls output format when the output is intended to be copied back into a lean file". That is different from the width in the InfoView. In my case (15 inch screen, for now), I use 80 columns in source files, and 47 columns in the InfoView. And, ideally, the same MessageData/Format would be rendered with different widths, depending on whether it currently is shown in the InfoView, or inserted into a Lean file.

The issue there is that the infoview generally has variable width and wraps content independently (and, I believe, does not re-format content on changing infoview width). So I'm not sure it makes sense in the first place to format for the infoview using any given width.

I can understand the notion of formatting for a completely separate document, though. But I'm not aware of any specific use cases. Both use cases I can think of involve putting the formatted output back into the lean file, as per inputWidth (namely, suggestions and autoformatting).

Maybe Verso is an example of formatting lean output for a fixed-width document, now that I think about it? Does that rely on ordinary formatting, or does it do its own special thing? Or, are verso artifacts generally also responsible for their own line-wrapping...?
I think for well-behaved variable-width content to work in the info view, it would need to have a Format -> HTML + CSS pipeline that preserves all the intended wrapping and indent semantics
What is the "this" there, exactly? Ah, I see :)

Thomas Murrills said:

The main proposal here is to make w := 0 in Std.Format.pretty correspond to infinite width,

If you just want an unwrapped string you can use fmt.pretty (w := 2^62) or whatever
Not with MessageData, it's a lot more awkward. You would lose hovers on Exprs that get split due to this width, I think.

Actually, I'm still a little hazy on what you mean earlier. Are you talking about what we'd need for "account for all possible widths as formatting with that width would", or "do not insert extra newlines"?

I think it's reasonable to not have unsightly newlines in the infoview even if we haven't figured out how to account for variable widths perfectly. That is, assuming a width of 120 in the infoview is definitely wrong, I believe :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

Thomas Murrills said:

Not with MessageData, it's a lot more awkward. You would lose hovers on Exprs that get split due to this width, I think.

To be explicit, here's a concrete example of where "just use a large width" breaks down for Exprs, which I've encountered in practice (two message lengths for comparison, as before); pretty is being used too deeply/lazily to be conveniently changed here (as far as I know).

import Lean
import Qq

open Lean Qq

/--
info: The instance hypothesis [(α : Type) →
   DecidableEq α] is in violation of the lorem ipsum dolor sit amet linter. Please change it immediately.
---
info: The instance hypothesis [(α : Type) → DecidableEq α]
-/
#guard_msgs in
run_cmd do
  let e := q(∀ α : Type, DecidableEq α)
  logInfo m!"The instance hypothesis {.sbracket m!"{e}"} is in violation of the \
    lorem ipsum dolor sit amet linter. Please change it immediately."
  logInfo m!"The instance hypothesis {.sbracket m!"{e}"}"

Thomas Murrills said:

The issue there is that the infoview generally has variable width and wraps content independently (and, I believe, does not re-format content on changing infoview width). So I'm not sure it makes sense in the first place to format for the infoview using any given width.

Eric Wieser said:

I think for well-behaved variable-width content to work in the info view, it would need to have a Format -> HTML + CSS pipeline that preserves all the intended wrapping and indent semantics

In my use-case (15 inch screen, only 47 columns for the InfoView when the editor has just over 80), just being able to set a fixed format width for the InfoView to a low enough value is already a boon. It makes a huge difference in readability. So having the format width automatically adapt to the current width of the InfoView is not necessary for a separate InfoView format width option to be useful. Automatically adapting the width may be a further option for some future RFC. I think it can be viewed as completely orthogonal, and could be disregarded for now.
I'm a bit confused, how do you control the number of columns of your infoview? I'm guessing you are not using VS code? :eyes:

Also, I do want to point out for this conversation, if you have a long expression and a tiny infoview, it does very much still get word-wrapped. Maybe not perfectly, but it is wrapped nonetheless. So simply not inserting extra newlines/acting as though we have "infinite width" already buys us a lot of portability across infoview widths.

Thomas Murrills said:

I'm a bit confused, how do you control the number of columns of your infoview? Are you not using VS code? :eyes:

VS Code, for now. By using the slider between the panes, or by using the VS Code command "Increase Editor width". So nothing that sets it to exactly 47 columns. The number 47 comes from experimentation. logInfo-ing a repeating sequence of "1234567890" or so, and seeing where it breaks.

Thomas Murrills said:

Also, I do want to point out for this conversation, if you have a long expression and a tiny infoview, it does very much still get word-wrapped. Maybe not perfectly, but it is wrapped nonetheless. So simply not inserting extra newlines/acting as though we have "infinite width" already buys us a lot of portability across infoview widths.



I think this shows that infinite width does not work at all as a default, let alone as a hard-coded value. All newlines seem to be optional in that example. And it shows how being able to set a smaller/different width can improve the experience, despite some lines still getting wrapped by the UI.

Thank you for this proposal!

Afaicr, 120 was just a guesstimate of the mode of the distribution of people's infoview widths. It may well be wrong. Using the real infoview width to pretty-print messages is indeed a missing feature. One reason for not adding it back in the day was that we'd need to ask the Lean server to re-print on every infoview resize event (modulo debouncing) since the pretty-printer is implemented in Lean. An alternative that has been discussed recently would be to run the pretty-printer directly from JS, somehow. One is to AI-port the algorithm to JS which @David Thrane Christiansen has done here. Another is to run it in the IR interpreter compiled to WASM, which @Emilio Jesús Gallego Arias has been experimenting with here.

make w := 0 in Std.Format.pretty correspond to infinite width

This sounds fine to me, though would not be necessary if we use the correct width in the end.

make infinite width the default when rendering MessageData

My instinct would be not to do this - the pretty-printing algorithm exists for a reason and does quite a bit better than the CSS-based line wrapping (EDIT: as demonstrated above :) ). It would be a shame to lose that.

Aha, I see! It's great to hear that there are experiments ongoing! :)

I see now my infinite-width default was far too naive. :) (As an even more common example of the sort of thing you're showing, Sebastian, very long lists would also now not be nice columns...)

In the meantime, I would definitely get some use out of w := 0 for infinite width + respecting the option value of format.width in MessageData. While we wait for the correct solution, we (downstream) could set format.width to 0 on certain MessageDatas by hand in cases where we know CSS-based line wrapping is going to outperform the best-effort default guess (e.g. #39296 and some other linters that are forced, one way or another, to include inline expressions or syntax). Then eventually we can deprecate that stopgap measure :) Though if there's a better solution in the interim, I'd definitely be interested; this is just the first thing that seemed reasonable to me.
In case you missed it, we can already use w := 2^62 to get the infinite width behavior you want from w := 0
(that's chosen to fit in boxed native integer without incurring GMP)

Somehow that seems ugly, but if it's an interim solution anyway then I guess I need to uncheck the stale "considered this option" box in my head :) (Didn't know about the "without incurring GMP part", though that wasn't a factor either way in how I was considering it :) )

I guess the only core change strictly necessary for this in practice is making MessageData respect format.width, then!

...Actually, I'm not sure it's easy to make MessageData respect the format.width in the necessary way. It's possible to make it respect it globally, but I don't think it composes easily: without a change to the formatting algorithm, it doesn't look like you can change the width "mid format" as we'd need to.
Without having looked at the code, presumably it's not MessageData that's relevant here; it's whatever code is calling MessageData.toFormat.pretty right before sending it to the infoview

The thing is that there's only one such point where prettyM is called, and it's at the top-level message. So you can maybe get the whole message to respect some ambient format.width, but you can't get nested expressions or messagedata to set their own format.width and be flattened, as far as I can see...
Could you link to where that happens?

Sure, it's msgToInteractive calling TaggedText.prettyTagged and then TaggetText.prettyTagged calling prettyM. Even if you alter the w passed to prettyM there, it seems like it's the same w for the whole message. (See also prettyM, and the pretty printing algorithm be just above it).)

(I did also alter prettyM to insert a token just before the text it's pretty-printing just to be sure, and that token was only inserted once in the above examples at the beginning of each logged message as expected.)

Though, in a different direction...I'm now wondering if the formatting of

The instance hypothesis [(α : Type) →
   DecidableEq α] is in violation of the lorem ipsum dolor sit amet linter. Please change it immediately.

is in fact breaking at the wrong places even for a width of 120. It seems like newlines are preferentially being inserted into the expression, rather than into the text. Would it make more sense for the text to break, rather than the expression?

Thomas Murrills said:

It seems like newlines are preferentially being inserted into the expression, rather than into the text. Would it make more sense for the text to break, rather than the expression?

I strongly guess that there is no prose/paragraph breaking in Format/MessageData at all. Example:

import Lean open Lean
run_cmd
  let fmt : Format := .text <| " ".intercalate <| List.replicate 50 "123456789"
  logInfo <| fmt.pretty (width := 30)

Even though (width := 30), the paragraph is not broken by format. No matter how wide the InfoView, breaking of the paragraph apparently only is done by CSS/UI. In my opinion, that's fine.

Instead, in core, the convention seems to be to always put stuff that could get longer on a separate indented line, like so:

import Lean import Qq open Lean Qq

/--
error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
  OfNat (Sort ?u.2) 23
numerals are polymorphic in Lean, but the numeral `23` cannot be used in a context where the expected type is
  Sort ?u.2
due to the absence of the instance above

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
-/
#guard_msgs in
#check (5 : 23)

/--
info: The instance hypothesis
  [(α : Type) → DecidableEq α]
is in violation of the lorem ipsum dolor sit amet linter. Please change it immediately.
-/
#guard_msgs in
run_cmd
  let e := q(∀ α : Type, DecidableEq α)
  logInfo <|
    m!"The instance hypothesis" ++
    indentD (.sbracket m!"{e}") ++ "\n" ++
    m!"is in violation of the lorem ipsum dolor sit amet linter. Please change it immediately."

In my optinion, that's more than fine, too.
So your examples all work as expected. But they are "wrong"/unidiomatic.

That's because " " is treated as a non-breaking space or rather, as a normal character without special handling. If you want a breaking space, you explicitly need to use Format.line (which is also what ppSpace uses):

import Lean open Lean

run_cmd
  let fmt : Format := .fill <| Std.Format.joinSep (List.replicate 50 "123456789") Format.line
  logInfo <| fmt.pretty (width := 30)

Sebastian Miele said:

So your examples all work as expected. But they are "wrong"/unidiomatic.

While the given example might indeed benefit from putting the expression on its own line, I disagree here in general, for two reasons:

First, inline expressions are a practical benefit in certain linter messages, especially when multiple usually-short expressions must be referenced. The real-life versions of the lorem ipsum toy example I’m giving are linters that may report on multiple instance binders; the options then become either to cave and make a maybe-long list of usually-short expressions, or to just grin and bear the weird newlines. Neither choice is great, but we’ve made both in practice; situations like this are not unique. Putting expressions on their own line should be a stylistic choice made by the message-writer, not a constraint imposed by the formatting infrastructure by default.

Second, it’s quite unintuitive behavior! And with no clear way to ameliorate it when programming. Even if you’d argue that the tactic syntax in #39296 should be put on its own line to be idiomatic, I believe the programmer is right in thinking that they shouldn’t have to, and shouldn’t have had broken formatting due to not making an idiomatic choice.

Broadly, I think in general textual spaces ought to be breaking by default. This is the case in every other formatting context that I can think of, and I’m not sure why formatting lean messages ought to be different. :)

One can probably write

def breakSpaces (f : String) : Format := …

or such without too much trouble (I may edit this to .fill in the definition when I’m no longer on mobile), but having to use this everywhere would definitely be a code smell.

(I’m guessing the practical reason spaces are non-breaking as of now is that we don’t have dynamic infoview wrapping yet, as mentioned earlier, so breaking would introduce more unexpected newlines than the status quo. I’m speaking only in principle above.)

Thanks, @Robin Arnez! So paragraphs indeed are possible! A small inconvenience arises, because MessageData.group does not have the behavior argument of Format.group.

import Lean import Qq open Lean Qq

def Std.Format.paragraphify (s : String) : Format := .joinSep (s.splitOn " ") .line

def Lean.MessageData.paragraphify : String → MessageData := .ofFormat ∘ .paragraphify
def Lean.MessageData.line : MessageData := .ofFormat .line

def Lean.MessageData.format' (msg : MessageData) : MetaM Format := do
  msg.format (ctx? := some ⟨← getEnv, ← getMCtx, ← getLCtx, ← getOptions⟩)

/--
info: The instance hypothesis (α : Type) → DecidableEq α is
in violation of the lorem ipsum dolor sit amet linter.
Please change it immediately.
-/
#guard_msgs (whitespace := exact) in
run_meta do
  let e := q(∀ α : Type, DecidableEq α)
  let msg : MessageData := .paragraphify "The instance hypothesis" ++ .line ++
    m!"{e}" ++ .line ++ .paragraphify "is in violation of the lorem" ++ .line ++
    .paragraphify "ipsum dolor sit amet linter. Please change it immediately."
  let fmt : Format := .group (behavior := .fill) <|← msg.format'
  logInfo <| fmt.pretty (width := 55)

Thomas Murrills said:

One can probably write

def breakSpaces (f : String) : Format := …

or such without too much trouble (I may edit this to .fill in the definition when I’m no longer on mobile), but having to use this everywhere would definitely be a code smell.

I called it paragraphify above, but breakSpaces is better. I guess it would be possible to implement a paragraph : Format → Format combinator that removes any code smell. I am currently not sure, if/how complicated it would get to "flatten" or remove Format.nests, or whether that would be necessary at all with the resulting surrounding .group. But it now think it probably is possible in a perfectly sensible way. I think I will try that.

And when the MessageData.group constructor also gets a behavior argument, then there can also be a paragraph : MessageData → MessageData without first converting the MessageData to a Format.

Thomas Murrills said:

Broadly, I think in general textual spaces ought to be breaking by default. This is the case in every other formatting context that I can think of, and I’m not sure why formatting lean messages ought to be different. :)

Think of display math mode in TeX or code blocks in Markdown. That are formatting contexts where line breaking is not the default, or in general would just garble the output. In typesetting systems there always is a clear distinction between paragraph stuff (horizontal mode in TeX) and other stuff that can appear vertically between paragraphs. Paragraph formatting / line breaking has very specific intricacies and demands.

Format (and by extension MessageData) is not made for paragraph formatting (although a basic form is possible with .group (behavior := .fill)). It is built for formatting of syntax trees at different widths and indents. In that context, space vs. newline can matter:

example: "a b" ≠ "a
b" := by decide

Using Format.text for paragraphs is sort of an abuse. And that certainly is the reason why the common idiom in Lean core seems to be to always put expressions on separate indented lines. That works reasonably well without Format/MessageData having proper support for paragraphs/prose.

In https://github.com/whxvd/paragraph-message I created a most basic form of MessageData.Paragraph that gets boiled down to MessageData in the very most plain way. On top of that, it defines pm!"" syntax that allows examples like:

def e₀ : Expr := q(∀ α: Type, DecidableEq α)
/--
info: The instance hypothesis [(α : Type) → DecidableEq α] is in
violation of the lorem ipsum dolor sit amet linter. Please
change it immediately.
-/
#guard_msgs (whitespace := exact) in
run_meta logInfo <|← Paragraph.pretty (width := 60) pm!"
  The instance hypothesis {.sbracket e₀} is in violation of the lorem
  ipsum dolor sit amet linter. Please change it immediately.
"

It uses the toolchain from lean#13914, which adds FlattenBehavior to MessageData.group.

Examples.lean has some more examples. It works reasonably well. It especially seems to fall back to rendering inline MessageData on separate lines in the middle of a paragraph, when the inline MessageData does not fit on a line, or when it has hard line breaks.

I tried more "intricate" forms of inlining of MessageData. I would rather like the expressions/MessageData to be indented by the usual 2 spaces when it has to appear on separate lines. But that has strange effects. I did not bother, yet, to describe these effects, because I still have to understand Format in detail, and produce/debug/understand those effects with examples directly stated in low-level Format.
Maybe Verso has solved rendering of elaborated Lean expressions inline in paragraphs? I could image the Verso maintainers to at least have a clear picture of the intricacies involved.
